title: Blog 1
content:
Managed Spot Training: Cost Savings Need Reliable Recovery Published on 3 November 2026 (Vietnam time). Original AWS Study Group VN post.
The experiments in this article are proposed and have no measured results.
Training cost includes model experiments, tuning and repeated runs rather than only the final successful job. This article examines SageMaker AI Managed Spot Training through both cost and completion reliability. It is a research article with a proposed experiment, not a claim of measured savings.
Managed Spot Training uses spare capacity that can be interrupted. A job may take longer to start or finish, and shortage does not automatically switch it to On-Demand. The practical question is where execution resumes after an interruption. Managed Spot Training
SageMaker synchronises checkpoint files between a container path and S3 and restores them when training restarts. A custom training script must still save and reload the correct state. Model weights alone may be insufficient: optimizer, learning-rate scheduler and step state can be needed for a faithful continuation. A checkpoint file’s presence does not prove successful recovery. Checkpoint configuration
Image: AWS Documentation, synchronising and restoring checkpoints. Original context. This is an AWS reference illustration, not a screenshot of a completed personal experiment.
A proposed comparison uses identical model, data and settings for On-Demand and Managed Spot Training. First, independently test restoring a known checkpoint. Then record wall-clock completion time, billable time, interruption count and final model quality. SageMaker job phases such as Starting, Training and Interrupted help explain timing. Job lifecycle
Checkpoint frequency is another variable. Long intervals risk repeating more work; frequent saves introduce write and synchronisation overhead. Compare several intervals on the same workload and record total runtime alongside work repeated. Do not report a percentage saving without the relevant job data and a comparable baseline.
Place inputs, checkpoints and model artifacts in clearly identified locations. Limit the training role to required S3 paths and review retained artifacts after the experiment. Storage and ancillary resources are part of the cost model rather than disappearing when compute finishes.
Spot is worth considering for recoverable experiments that tolerate waiting. Deadline-sensitive work must weigh the discount against delayed completion. This research supports that decision framework; it does not establish the savings of an unexecuted experiment.

title: Overview and Completion Criteria
content:
Product and Users AUREL is an original demonstration brand with a custom dark/gold interface. Guests can browse 100 Vietnamese dishes and supplementary items, view credited venue photographs, submit reservation requests, and send messages. Staff accounts are provisioned via Cognito and assigned to the admin group to manage data.
Reservation requests are set to pending upon receipt. Staff then decide whether to confirm or cancel. This is an important business distinction: receiving a successful form submission notification does not mean the restaurant has confirmed the reservation.
Technology Next.js 15.5.28, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zod, AWS SDK v3, Node.js 22, pnpm 11.25.0. Lambda runs on arm64 with 256 MB memory and a 20-second timeout in Singapore. Explicit access control boundaries between public and admin APIs. Capacity protection via transactions within a single slot; UUID deduplication preventing duplicate requests. Infrastructure templates, build/deploy instructions, testing, observability, and cleanup procedures. Limitations to Understand Before Starting SES remains in the sandbox; admin MFA lacks a handling UI; no outbox or queue has been deployed. The capacity model only applies to the same time slot and does not account for dining duration. Venue photographs are curated from multiple locations rather than an actual physical AUREL restaurant.

title: Proposal
content:
Aurel Restaurant Website 1. Solution Overview Aurel is a contemporary Vietnamese restaurant website designed to turn online visitors into restaurant guests. The current site presents the Aurel story, seasonal menu, dining space, contact information, and a clear route to make a reservation. Its visual direction focuses on thoughtful dining, Vietnamese flavours, and a warm, intimate atmosphere.
The proposed solution develops this website into a reliable digital guest journey. Visitors can discover the restaurant, browse the menu, view the gallery, find opening hours and location details, and submit a reservation request. Restaurant staff can review requests and manage reservation availability through a protected administration area.
2. Objectives and Scope Objectives Create a responsive, accessible website that reflects Aurel’s contemporary Vietnamese dining identity. Help guests quickly find the menu, opening hours, location, contact details, and reservation experience. Provide a simple reservation-request workflow that reduces manual messages and phone calls. Use managed AWS services so that the website can be deployed, monitored, and scaled without maintaining servers. Give restaurant staff a secure way to review reservation requests and manage website content in later phases. Scope Included in phase 1
Public pages for Home, Menu, Gallery, Story, Contact, and Reservation. Mobile-friendly navigation and clear calls to action. A reservation form that records guest name, contact details, preferred date and time, party size, and special notes. Confirmation and notification workflow for submitted reservation requests. Basic staff administration and operational monitoring. Not included in phase 1
Online payment, food delivery, loyalty points, and a full table-layout management system. Integration with a third-party point-of-sale system. Real-time automatic confirmation without a staff review step. 3. Problems to Solve Problem Effect on the guest or restaurant Proposed response Restaurant information is scattered across social channels or messages. Guests may not find the menu, opening hours, address, or reservation method quickly. Maintain one clear, responsive website as the main source of information. Reservation requests can be handled manually through calls and chat messages. Staff may need to re-enter details, while guests may wait for a response. Provide a structured reservation form and notify staff of each request. A visual dining concept needs a strong online presentation. Guests may not understand the Aurel experience before visiting. Use the existing story, menu, gallery, and call-to-action pages to communicate the brand consistently. A small restaurant team should not need to operate servers. Infrastructure maintenance takes time away from guest service. Use managed and serverless AWS services for hosting, APIs, storage, and monitoring. 4. Preliminary Solution Architecture The solution uses a serverless AWS architecture. The public website is deployed with AWS Amplify Hosting. A reservation request is sent through Amazon API Gateway to AWS Lambda, validated, and stored in Amazon DynamoDB. Staff receive a notification through Amazon Simple Email Service (SES). Amazon Cognito protects the administration area, while Amazon CloudWatch collects logs and alarms.
AWS Services AWS Amplify Hosting — builds and hosts the public website with continuous deployment. Amazon CloudFront — delivers the website quickly through the Amplify hosting distribution. Amazon API Gateway — exposes a controlled HTTPS endpoint for reservation submissions. AWS Lambda — validates reservation data and coordinates backend actions without a server to manage. Amazon DynamoDB — stores reservation requests in a flexible, scalable database. Amazon SES — sends a notification to staff and, in a later phase, an acknowledgement to the guest. Amazon Cognito — controls access to the staff administration area. Amazon CloudWatch — records errors, request activity, and operational alarms. AWS WAF — optional protection for the public application as traffic grows. 5. Implementation Plan and Timeline Week Milestone Deliverables 1 Discovery and content planning Confirm restaurant information, page structure, menu data, brand tone, and reservation requirements. 2 User interface and public website Complete responsive Home, Menu, Gallery, Story, and Contact pages; test navigation on mobile and desktop. 3 Reservation workflow Build the reservation form, API endpoint, validation, DynamoDB storage, and staff-notification flow. 4 Security, testing, and launch Protect staff access with Cognito, add CloudWatch monitoring, test reservation scenarios, and publish the production version. Ongoing Improvement and content maintenance Update seasonal menu content, review reservation data, improve search visibility, and add features based on guest feedback. 6. Cost Estimation The following is a planning estimate for a low-traffic restaurant website. Actual charges depend on traffic, data retention, email volume, AWS Region, and any free-tier eligibility. Domain registration, tax, and optional third-party services are not included.
Component Estimated monthly cost Notes Amplify Hosting and delivery USD 0–8 Depends on build minutes, storage, and data transfer. API Gateway and Lambda USD 0–3 Suitable for a low volume of reservation submissions. DynamoDB USD 0–3 Low-volume reservation records and on-demand capacity. SES and CloudWatch USD 0–3 Notification email and basic operational monitoring. Estimated total USD 0–17 / month Validate the final configuration with AWS Pricing Calculator before launch. 7. Risks and Mitigation Risk Impact Mitigation Incorrect or duplicate reservation requests Guests may receive unclear booking status. Validate the form, use a staff-review status, and show that a request is not confirmed until staff respond. Exposure of personal contact details Guest trust and privacy may be affected. Store only necessary information, restrict staff access with Cognito, and follow a data-retention policy. Spam or automated form submissions Staff may receive unnecessary notifications. Add server-side validation, rate limiting, and AWS WAF rules if traffic requires them. Service or deployment errors The website or reservation form may be unavailable. Use CloudWatch alarms, deployment rollback, and regular reservation-flow testing. Inaccurate menu or opening-hour information Guests may have a poor experience before arriving. Assign an owner for content updates and review seasonal content before publishing. Costs increase with traffic or new features Operating costs may exceed the initial estimate. Set AWS Budgets alerts, review usage monthly, and use managed serverless services that scale gradually. Expected Outcomes The completed solution will give Aurel a cohesive online presence that reflects its dining experience and makes reservations easier to manage. Guests will have a clear path from discovering the restaurant to submitting a booking request, while staff will receive structured information in one place. The architecture can grow later to support automatic confirmations, table availability, online events, loyalty features, or point-of-sale integrations.

title: Blog 2
content:
Lambda and SQS: Why Successful Work Can Run Again Published on 5 November 2026 (Vietnam time). Original AWS Study Group VN post.
The experiments in this article are proposed and have no measured results.
An order-processing or sensor-data application can acknowledge incoming work quickly and process it later through SQS and Lambda. The difficult part is partial failure: some messages may complete before another fails. This research examines retry behaviour and correctness without claiming a deployed SQS pipeline in AUREL.
An SQS event source mapping polls messages and invokes Lambda in batches. Successfully processed messages are deleted, but delivery is at least once and duplicates remain possible. Applications must be designed for repeated processing. Lambda with SQS
Consider a batch of ten messages where the sixth fails. Under default failure behaviour, the batch can reappear after visibility timeout, including messages whose business actions succeeded. An unconditional counter increment or transaction creation could therefore run twice.
Partial batch responses let the function identify failed messages. Both ReportBatchItemFailures on the event source mapping and the correct function response are necessary. Changing only the function code is insufficient. Partial batch error handling
Image: AWS Documentation, event source mapping in the SQS tutorial. Original tutorial. The image is a reference, not evidence of a personally executed test.
Reducing unnecessary retries does not remove the need for idempotency. Use a business request identifier and design for simultaneous workers and failures between the business effect and completion marker. A separate check-then-write sequence can race. The hardest boundary is an external effect that cannot participate in the database transaction; acknowledge and test that uncertainty rather than promising exactly-once behaviour.
A proposed experiment mixes valid messages, deliberately invalid messages and duplicate business IDs. Compare invocation/message counts with the final number of business outcomes. Verify that repeatedly failing messages reach the configured dead-letter queue. Function timeout, visibility timeout and redrive policy must be assessed together. SQS configuration for Lambda
Persistent poison messages can increase compute and logging cost. Scope the execution role to the queue and result store and avoid logging sensitive payloads. Queueing separates reception from processing; application-level state and failure handling still determine whether results are correct.

title: Architecture and Data Flow
content:
AUREL Architecture Diagram Flow ③ is the path from Next.js BFF to API Gateway for administrative requests. The browser calls API Gateway directly for menu, reservations, and contact. Arrow ⑦ in the image connects Cognito to S3 Media. The actual flow is that Cognito issues an access token to the admin, Lambda writes images to S3 using its IAM execution role, and the browser then reads images via presigned GET URLs. S3 Media stores files, DynamoDB stores application data, and SES delivers emails.
CloudWatch centralizes logs and operational metrics. Section 5.9 details the access logs, dashboard, and four configured alarms.
Guest Flow The browser loads HTML, JavaScript, images, and fonts from Amplify Hosting over HTTPS. GET /menu calls API Gateway directly. Lambda queries the menu partition and returns currently available items. POST /reservations is validated against schema, consent, honeypot, IP/email rate limits, and Vietnam date-time. DynamoDB writes the request and increments the seat counter within the same transaction, limited to 24 seats per time slot. Resubmitting with an existing saved UUID will return the request ID without incrementing seats again. For new requests, Lambda attempts to send a receipt email via SES after the transaction succeeds. The restaurant confirms bookings separately. If sending fails, the request is still preserved. SES is currently in sandbox mode, so it can only send to verified addresses/domains or the mailbox simulator. POST /contact saves customer messages. Guest data cannot be read via public APIs. Admin and Media Flow The browser sends login credentials over HTTPS to Next.js BFF. BFF authenticates with Cognito and retains the access token in an HttpOnly cookie (Secure in production, SameSite=Strict). When calling admin APIs, BFF forwards the access token in the Authorization header. API Gateway’s JWT authorizer verifies the signature using Cognito’s JWKS public key, issuer, audience or client ID, and expiration. Lambda further verifies token_use=access and the admin group membership.
When an admin uploads dish images, the request passes through Next.js BFF and API Gateway. Lambda validates JPEG, PNG, or WebP files up to 2 MB, then stores them under the menu-images/ prefix in the private bucket. DynamoDB stores the image path alongside the dish record. When guests view the menu, Lambda verifies that the dish is currently active and the image version is current before issuing a presigned GET URL.
The experimental feature at /admin/media uses 120-second presigned PUT URLs and 900-second presigned GET URLs for direct browser-to-S3 transfers. Experimental files under uploads/ expire after 30 days. The Media bucket blocks public access and enforces HTTPS.
The Lambda execution role also possesses CRUD permissions on the application’s DynamoDB table and send permissions via the configured SES identity.
DynamoDB Data Model pk sk Contents / Access menu Dish ID MenuItem; public menu query filtered by available reservations UUID Request details and status; read by admin only contacts UUID Messages; read by admin only slots YYYY-MM-DD#HH:mm Seats counter, conditionally updated limits Hash + time bucket Hit count and expires TTL The table enables encryption and PITR on-demand. Adapter queries support pagination, but the dashboard currently fetches the full list; when scaling up, paginated APIs and date filtering are needed. TTL is a delayed cleanup mechanism, not a precision timer. The pending status still holds seats; physical tables and overlapping dining timeframes are not modeled.
Why Choose These Services? Service Rationale Trade-offs Amplify Hosting Managed HTTPS, CDN, Next SSR support, Git-based builds Framework constraints and build/SSR/bandwidth costs API Gateway HTTP API JWT authorizer, CORS, throttling; simple operations Cannot attach AWS WAF directly like REST API Lambda Auto-scales on demand; serverless Cold starts, timeout, concurrency quota DynamoDB Transactions and conditional writes, on-demand Must design around access patterns; no SQL joins Cognito Managed identities, admin groups, and tokens MFA challenges require additional UI development S3 Private media, presigned URLs, lifecycle policies Presigned URLs act as bearer capabilities until expiry SES Integrated AWS email, pay-per-use Sandbox limits, deliverability, and retries need handling CloudWatch Centralized logs, metrics, dashboards, and alarms Requires threshold tuning and alert routing plans CodeCommit / CloudFormation Private repository and reviewable infrastructure Permissions and update workflows differ from GitHub App Lambda is not placed in a VPC merely to add diagram components: the application connects to public AWS service endpoints and has no database inside a private subnet. DynamoDB and S3 are regional managed services, not resources inside a private subnet. If private dependencies are added later, VPCs, endpoints, NAT, and costs should then be evaluated.
Deployment Flow A git push to the CodeCommit main branch triggers Amplify to build and deploy the interface along with Next.js BFF. Backend and infrastructure are updated separately via AWS CLI using SAM/CloudFormation templates. The Artifacts bucket stores Lambda packages and deployment files. The Media bucket serves files uploaded by the application.

title: Blog 3
content:
Optimising Athena: Data Layout Can Matter More Than SQL Changes Published on 8 November 2026 (Vietnam time). Original AWS Study Group VN post.
The experiments in this article are proposed and have no measured results.
For the same analytical result, how much can storage layout change the amount of data read? This article studies Athena SQL queries billed by scanned data. Other Athena capacity/pricing options exist, so estimates must identify the chosen mode. No comparative benchmark is claimed here. Athena pricing
Two distinct variables are columnar format and partitioning. Parquet allows a query reading selected fields to skip unrelated columns. Its metadata can also help eliminate some data blocks when predicates permit. This supports a hypothesis of improvement over row-oriented text, not a guarantee that every query becomes faster. Columnar formats
Partitioning narrows the data range. For daily logs, a suitable predicate on the partition key can restrict reads to relevant days. Creating date-based S3 directories alone is insufficient; Athena table configuration and metadata must reflect that organisation. Partitioning
Image: AWS Big Data Blog, a reference pipeline with conversion and partitioning. Original article. This older reference illustrates the concept rather than claiming a newly deployed personal architecture.
A proposed experiment compares identical data in three layouts: unpartitioned CSV, unpartitioned Parquet and date-partitioned Parquet. Contents and types must be equivalent. Use queries selecting a few columns for one day, aggregating a month and reading most data. Record bytes scanned, execution duration and returned results for each case.
Control result reuse, repeat runs and confirm result equivalence before interpreting timing. Otherwise a cached response or a changed dataset can appear to be a layout improvement. Excessively fine partitions and many small files can add metadata and file-open overhead. Partition keys should follow real query patterns. AWS performance guidance
A full comparison includes conversion work, duplicate optimised storage and pipeline maintenance. Use public data for the lab, restrict access to its bucket and manage query output storage. Clean up both intermediate data and query results after retaining the evidence needed for the comparison.
The research goal is to state which query shapes benefit, what trade-offs arise and which measurements support the conclusion. “Parquet is always better” is not an adequate experimental finding.

Verify BUILD/DEPLOY/VERIFY stages, open the URL, and cross-check API responses. In the actual deployment, job 5 succeeded with commit ffe7deaa88b7090ad0f10ca60ed1f86f3cc16d8b.
Environment Configuration Variable Source / Rule DATA_MODE aws API_BASE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL ApiUrl, no trailing slash COGNITO_CLIENT_ID, COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID Backend outputs APP_AWS_REGION ap-southeast-1 APP_ORIGIN Exact frontend origin scripts/amplify-env.mjs only writes allowed configurations to .env.production. Updating Source Code Code.S3 only loads the source during initial repository creation. Replacing the ZIP in S3 and updating the stack will not update the Git history. Subsequent updates must use Git/CodeCommit with temporary IAM sessions, pushing to the main branch; Amplify will build automatically. If the account cannot connect to CodeCommit, use the GitHub alternative outlined in the application README and amplify.yaml template; never make the repository public with .env files. This alternative path has not been tested in a new account.

The report is exported from Hugo to a minimal Next.js host on a separate CodeCommit report branch, attached to the Amplify report branch of the existing app. The restaurant’s main branch and backend remain unchanged.
The host preserves the HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and fonts of the Hugo template; routes serve HTML from public, and static assets pass through Hosting. The configuration preserves trailing slashes and packages HTML within server trace. Large downloadable files are split when stored in Git. title: Security and Well-Architected Review
content:
Identity and Access Control Guests use public routes for the menu, published dish photos, reservations, and contact. Administrators must have a valid unexpired token with the expected issuer/client and admin group membership. HttpOnly cookies reduce direct JavaScript token access; Secure, SameSite=Strict and Origin checks protect BFF mutations. Tokens are not stored in localStorage. Logout attempts GlobalSignOut, but issued JWTs may still be accepted by Gateway until expiration; immediate revocation is not claimed.
Cognito MFA is currently set to OFF. Do not set MFA to REQUIRED before the UI handles challenges, as this will prevent admin logins. Subsequent priorities are TOTP/challenge support, account recovery, and thorough testing before enforcing MFA.
Runtime IAM The Lambda role only accesses the project table, S3 uploads/, menu-images/, and the designated SES identity. However, the template currently uses DynamoDBCrudPolicy, which grants broader actions than the runtime actually needs. This should be narrowed upon review to Query, GetItem, PutItem, DeleteItem, UpdateItem, and relevant data operations within TransactWriteItems, scoped strictly to the specific table ARN; do not grant account-wide DynamoDB access.
A narrower policy example for review (not yet applied to the current stack):
{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["dynamodb:Query", "dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:DeleteItem", "dynamodb:UpdateItem"], "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:REGION:ACCOUNT:table/YOUR_TABLE" } TransactWriteItems permissions are authorized based on its constituent component operations; do not invent non-existent IAM actions simply because the API name is TransactWriteItems. Deployment roles have different needs from runtime roles and require a separately reviewed deployment policy.
Data and Networking S3 enables all four Block Public Access settings, SSE-S3, enforced Object Ownership, and non-TLS denial. DynamoDB enables SSE and PITR. No public database password exists. Presigned URLs are not public objects, but anyone with a valid URL can use it; do not expose these URLs in reports or logs.
Public endpoints are necessary for guest access. Lambda does not have a public IP directly accessed by guests; invocation is handled by Gateway. No custom VPC is deployed. Only add private subnets/endpoints when justified by networking requirements, considering NAT/endpoint costs.
API logs record only metadata, omitting forms, emails, phone numbers, Cookies, or Authorization headers. Guest records currently lack a complete retention/deletion workflow; formal data policies are required before production operations.
Pillar Review Pillar Implementation Limitations / Improvements Operational Excellence IaC, pipelines, tests, logs, and runbooks Standardize rollbacks and verified small changes Security Cognito/JWT/group, cookies, private S3, no hardcoded keys MFA, non-root deployment access, narrowed IAM actions Reliability DDB transactions/PITR, managed services Outbox/queue, restore drills, no multi-region DR Performance Efficiency WebP, thumbnails, self-hosted fonts, arm64 Load testing needed; dashboard requires API pagination Cost Optimization On-demand billing, 30-day lifecycle, 14-day log retention Finalize Calculator estimate and Budget alerts Sustainability Demand-based compute, smaller image bytes and font payload Measure traffic and remove unused resources References Least privilege and temporary credentials IAM DynamoDB actions

Test Results Table Group Recorded Results Scope Local 30 tests; typecheck/build; 28 HTTP smoke assertions Prior to venue gallery release; DynamoDB transactions mocked AWS Backend 14 successful checks Cognito/access token, ID token rejection, persistence/status/idempotency, live S3 PUT/GET, contact Menu Release Public/admin APIs return 100 dishes, 100 byte-matched images, 7 HTTP 200 pages HTTP/assets/auth validation, without browser automation Venue Gallery Release 12 cards, 8 venue images, 20 byte-matched assets, menu remains at 100 HTTP and server-rendered HTML Monitoring See updated evidence in section 5.9 Simulated alarm transitions do not imply real outages Evidence Links Browser checks were previously conducted on the initial deployment: BFF login, dashboard, logout, and reservations. Those screenshots predate the 100-dish menu update; they should not be used to claim that all interactions of the new gallery have been verified.
Reproducible Negative Requests export API_URL=YOUR_API_URL curl -i "$API_URL/admin/reservations" curl -i -X POST "$API_URL/reservations" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{}' curl -i -X POST "$API_URL/reservations" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{bad-json' curl -i -X OPTIONS "$API_URL/menu" \ -H 'Origin: https://untrusted.example' \ -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: GET' Expected responses: 401, 400, and 400 respectively; untrusted origins do not receive an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header granting access. HTTP 200 for OPTIONS does not mean the origin is allowed. Do not run heavy load tests against the public demo.
State-Changing Tests — Lab Account Only Use the form with a verified email or SES mailbox simulator, with a date 1–90 days in the future and at least 30 minutes in advance. Record the returned UUID, log in to admin, confirm, reload, and then cancel. Reconcile DynamoDB records and the slot counter. Resubmitting with the same UUID returns the same request; changing data requires a new UUID.
To test real concurrency, isolate a dedicated slot and send concurrent requests with total guests exceeding 24. After testing, verify total seats do not exceed 24 and no orphaned partial records exist. This concurrency load test has not been executed on live DynamoDB in the current evidence set.
Do not wipe the table to clean up tests. Clean up only the specific UUIDs created during testing; cancel first to release capacity, then delete test records if needed. Retain status logs without storing tokens or personal data in the report.
Remaining UI Checks Direct testing is still needed on Windows/Chrome/Edge, iOS/Android devices, lightbox keyboard navigation, screen readers, color contrast, and forms on small screens. These cannot be assumed to pass solely from HTTP 200 responses or successful builds.

title: Logs, Metrics, Alarms and Runbook
content:
Supplementary Operational Configuration The aurel-observability stack provisioned a dashboard, four alarms, and a dedicated log group. API stage access logging is configured via CLI outside the original backend SAM template and should be reapplied after any stage changes.
Reproducing the Configuration Download the two files into the same directory. API_ID is the API identifier from ApiUrl; obtain FUNCTION_NAME from your lab’s Lambda/CloudFormation outputs.
aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name aurel-observability \ --template-file observability.json \ --parameter-overrides ApiId=YOUR_API_ID FunctionName=YOUR_FUNCTION_NAME python3 configure-api-logs.py --api-id YOUR_API_ID aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-name-prefix aurel-observability- aws logs tail /aurel/aurel-observability/http-api --since 10m aws logs tail /aws/lambda/aurel-backend-api --since 10m Logs contain only requestId, requestTime, routeKey, status, responseLength, and integrationLatency, with a 14-day retention period. Cookies, Authorization headers, and request bodies are omitted. Lambda maintains its separate log group. requestTime retains the original timestamp provided by API Gateway; correlate it with event timestamps in CloudWatch.
Metrics and Alarms Alarm Metric / Statistic Condition Remediation LambdaErrors AWS/Lambda Errors, Sum >=1 in 5 minutes Inspect timeouts/runtime failures and Lambda logs LambdaThrottles Throttles, Sum >=1 in 5 minutes Review concurrency/quotas and reduce burst limits Api5xx AWS/ApiGateway 5xx, Sum >=1 in 5 minutes Correlate requestId across API and Lambda logs ApiLatency Latency, Average >=2000 ms across 2 consecutive 5-minute windows Check cold starts, DynamoDB, SES, and traffic load Missing data is treated as notBreaching; do not rely on this setting as proof that the system is always healthy. An idle system without traffic may still show an OK status. The Average latency alarm is not an indicator of p95 performance. A handler returning JSON 500 may not increment Lambda Errors; the API 5xx metric adds visibility into caught runtime failures.
The chart above was retrieved using GetMetricWidgetImage from CloudWatch, not a manual Console screenshot. 4xx errors during testing include unauthenticated requests and invalid bodies generated intentionally during negative testing; they do not reflect actual customer incidents.
Evidence and Alert Limitations The file monitoring.json documents stack status, thresholds, log configuration, and state transition history. The SetAlarmState test transitioned Api5xx to ALARM and back to OK to verify the state management pipeline. This was a simulation; actual threshold breaches and external notification deliveries under real 5xx conditions have not been verified.
Currently, AlarmActions and OKActions are empty with no active SNS subscriptions. Therefore, alarms evaluate within CloudWatch but do not dispatch emails. To deliver alerts outside the Console, an SNS topic and subscriptions must be created, verified via AWS confirmation email, and tested end-to-end; simply creating alarms does not constitute a complete email alert mechanism.
Runbook Identify the alarm, time window, and traffic volume; distinguish 4xx user input errors from 5xx system failures. Search for the requestId in access logs and correlate timestamps with Lambda logs, Duration, and Throttles. If a new deployment introduced errors, compare commits/jobs and promote a stable commit through the pipeline; never wipe the database as a troubleshooting measure. If SES fails, verify sandbox status, identity verification, and quotas; reservation requests are preserved in admin, so avoid creating duplicate UUIDs merely to re-trigger emails. Following remediation, verify with both valid and invalid requests, review metrics and alarm recovery status, and document root causes and preventative actions. title: Resource Cleanup
content:
Principles and Inventory These instructions target the reader’s lab account. Do not execute cleanup on an active demo without having decided to retire the service. Deleting a CloudFormation stack does not mean all resources are removed: the DynamoDB table, media/artifact buckets, and CodeCommit repository have a Retain deletion policy.
Prior to deletion, export the physical resource inventory and identify ownership. Back up necessary data to an authorized private location and confirm backups can be read. A real-world restore drill has not yet been conducted to empirically validate RTO/RPO.
aws cloudformation list-stack-resources --stack-name aurel-backend aws cloudformation list-stack-resources --stack-name aurel-frontend aws cloudformation list-stack-resources --stack-name aurel-artifacts aws cloudformation list-stack-resources --stack-name aurel-observability Lab Cleanup Sequence Stop new pipelines/builds; record AppId and resource IDs prior to deletion. Archive report source/builds, then delete the aurel-report-branch stack and the source report branch if no longer needed. Do not delete the shared Amplify app or the restaurant’s main branch. Any empty buckets remaining from CloudFront trials must be inventoried separately by stack. Delete the frontend stack; wait for DELETE_COMPLETE. CodeCommit has a Retain policy and requires separate cleanup. Delete the backend stack; wait for completion. Stack-owned Cognito users, SES identities, and log groups will be removed; the DynamoDB table and media bucket will remain. Delete the observability stack to clean up alarms, dashboards, and API access logs. Only delete if logs are no longer required for analysis. For retained S3 buckets, check versioning, all versions/delete markers, and multipart uploads. After backing up, empty the bucket, then delete it. The command rm –recursive does not delete all versions in a versioned bucket. Delete only the specific retained DynamoDB tables and repositories identified in your inventory; review any manual backups/exports and their associated fees. Clean up the artifact bucket, then delete the artifacts stack; handle the retained bucket if detached from stack management. Check out-of-stack Amplify logs, SNS subscriptions/Budgets added later, and resources in other regions. Do not delete unrelated project resources. Sample stack deletion commands, to be executed only after deciding to conclude the lab and completing backups:
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name aurel-frontend aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name aurel-frontend aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name aurel-backend aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name aurel-backend aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name aurel-observability aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name aurel-observability Retained resource deletion is intentionally not automated via wildcards due to the risk of deleting out-of-scope data. Verify actual resource states and check AWS Billing after data updates; closing the browser does not stop charges. This report does not claim that the infrastructure serving the live demo has been deleted.

title: Troubleshooting and Technical Lessons
content:
Project Troubleshooting Scenarios Situation Diagnosis Resolution and Evidence Nested source ZIP folder Build could not locate package.json at root Created package-source script to produce a clean archive at the root Reserved concurrency 10 conflicted with quota of 10 Did not leave unreserved capacity Removed reserved concurrency, retained API gateway throttling, and documented account limits Origin configuration changes caused CORS/BFF errors Public API and BFF have different request pathways Aligned API/S3 CORS with the same origin, updated APP_ORIGIN, and rebuilt the public environment SES sandbox restrictions Sending capability does not cover arbitrary recipient addresses Verified sender identity, tested with mailbox simulator, persisted requests prior to notification, and clearly documented sandbox mode Documentation commits triggered app builds Branch pipeline did not reliably recognize skip markers Stopped docs-only build jobs; separated report repository from the application repository Legacy seed and 100-item catalogue Custom items added by users must not be erased Implemented migration backup and recognized default sample dishes while preserving other data Desiring real photos from different locations Misrepresentation risk regarding branding/venue Labeled images as documentary/inspiration assets with source attribution and licenses per photo Transferable Lessons Tracing requests along data pathways helps identify whether errors originate in the browser, BFF, API Gateway, Lambda, or database. A successful build does not prove durable form submission; an HTTP 200 does not prove responsiveness or accessibility. An SES delivery failure does not mean the reservation transaction failed.
Least privilege requires examining individual actions and resources, not just policy names. Managed services do not automatically satisfy all security requirements. Retain protects data but introduces operational cleanup and billing oversight responsibilities.
Prioritized Future Roadmap Migrate deployment operations away from root, narrow IAM policies, implement and test MFA. Complete external notification delivery and set an agreed AWS Budget threshold. Introduce Outbox/SQS/DLQ, handle duplicate messages, and reconcile pending outbox records. Implement API pagination, rule-based pending reservation expiry, and modeling for tables/dining durations. Run controlled load testing, restore drills, and observe empirical p95 latency and cost measurements. Perform testing across Windows/mobile/accessibility, and add walkthrough video demonstrations and personally revised architecture diagrams. This represents a technical roadmap rather than a list of currently implemented features. Directly attaching AWS WAF to an HTTP API is not supported; a compatible protective architecture must be designed first.
